item.title: USDA Cyber Incident Disrupts Farmer Payments
item.description:
Farmers are having trouble accessing loan and payment services after a cybersecurity incident forced the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) to take several applications offline this week. The disruption comes as farmers approach enrollment deadlines for federal support programs, while DTN has reported delays to loans, payments and conservation work.

Who was behind the intrusion, how they infiltrated the system and the full extent of the intrusion remain unknown.

As per an internal email sent on November 16 by Chris Rottler, acting assistant chief information officer at the Farm Production and Conservation (FPAC) Business Center, the department had detected a security incident after which the staff was instructed to reset database passwords across all environments. This process also required applications to be restarted.

Farmer Loans and Payments Disrupted

The outages affected many services, including Farm Service Agency (FSA) loan software, the Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) ProTracts payment system and mapping software. Some employees also reported problems connecting to the department’s virtual private network (VPN).

FPAC Undersecretary Richard Fordyce confirmed on November 20 that it was a cyber threat and not a software update, stating that: “There was no Personally Identifiable Information (PII). No data was lost because the systems that protect against cybersecurity threats worked.”

Fordyce expected most systems to resume operations by Friday evening, with work continuing over the weekend if needed. However, reports citing two former USDA officials said hackers had accessed the farmer-payment system.

The outages have struck the department at a crucial time when farmers are dealing with deadlines to sign up for federal support programs. The Agriculture Risk Coverage (ARC) and Price Loss Coverage (PLC) programs help farmers manage losses when crop prices or farm income fall, and enrollment for the 2026 programs closes on December 11. Dairy farmers have a separate deadline of December 18 to enroll in the 2027 Dairy Margin Coverage (DMC) program that helps protect them when milk prices fall or feed costs rise.

Food Supply Risks No Longer Limited to Data Theft

A recently released Government Accountability Office (GAO) report has highlighted cybersecurity-related concerns across the food and agriculture sector. USDA and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had met most of 16 federal requirements, but five involving emergency preparedness and information sharing remained partly or fully unmet.

GAO’s report warned that attacks could interfere with equipment controlling irrigation, fertilizing and food production, potentially affecting food safety and public trust. GAO also identified gaps in real-time threat sharing with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“We also found that USDA and FDA don’t provide CISA with real-time information about threats. Having this information would help agencies to respond. As the food and agriculture sector faces increased cybersecurity risks, it is critical to ensure that the right resources are allocated to address these threats,” the agency noted.

The threat is not just about computers being unavailable, as we’ve seen in the recently reported attacks in Europe where hackers changed supermarket refrigeration settings, forcing stores to discard food. The USDA disruption has affected financial services for farmers, but attacks on connected agricultural equipment could reach the farms, storage facilities and food businesses too. So, the consequences of such incidents could extend well beyond an IT outage, causing much higher losses.

Experts’ Commentary:

Security experts shared their comments with Hackread.com, saying the USDA incident highlights how cyberattacks can affect people who depend on government services, not just the systems themselves.

John Strand, Owner of Black Hills Information Security, said agriculture is often overlooked when people discuss critical infrastructure, despite its role in feeding the population.

“When people think about critical infrastructure and cyberattacks, they usually think about the power grid, water treatment facilities, dams, and things of that nature. And they’re absolutely right. But what a lot of people don’t think about is farming and ranching.”

“At the end of the day, one of the most critical functions of any country is its ability to feed its citizens. Agriculture is absolutely critical infrastructure, and we need to start treating it that way.”

Seemant Sehgal, Founder and CEO of BreachLock, focused on the password resets that caused the USDA applications to go offline. He said the incident raises questions about how well the department understands the connections between its systems.

“A blanket database password reset across every environment usually means nobody could say with confidence which credentials the intruder had touched. When one reset can take down farm loan and crop insurance payments, the dependencies between those systems were never mapped well enough to be changed safely. GAO’s findings on missed emergency exercises suggest these agencies are learning how their systems fail while they are failing, and farmers waiting on payments cover the cost of that education.”

Joshua Marpet, Senior Product Security Consultant at Finite State, pointed to the consequences of failing to meet basic cybersecurity requirements. He said these requirements are meant to make systems harder to attack, even if they cannot guarantee complete protection.

“Requirements are just that. They are the minimum requirements to not get hacked, to be at least marginally secure, to be harder to reach, and harder to break into. Not impossible, mind you. Just harder. When requirements aren’t met, then the safety margin is reduced. When people’s farm loans and personal data are at risk, reducing that safety margin seems like a bad idea.”

(Photo by Mark Stebnicki via Pexels)

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: When Executive Impersonation Spreads Across Multiple Platforms
item.description:
In a hypothetical scenario, a company discovers a social media profile using its chief executive’s name and photograph. At first, the problem appears limited to one account. Then a partner encounters a website carrying the same photograph and a copied company description. Even if the profile disappears, the website may remain available to anyone searching for the business.

Executive impersonation can involve several distinct sources: accounts that appear to speak for a person, websites that appear to represent a business, and copied material that lends either one credibility. Understanding those differences helps security and communications teams assess the exposure without mistaking the first visible profile for the entire problem.

Why an impersonation case may extend beyond one profile

A fake profile is often the most noticeable part of an impersonation problem because it can approach customers or partners directly. Its name, photograph and biography may resemble a real executive’s public presence. But a profile is an account controlled through a particular platform. A website is a separate destination, and copied identity material can appear on either. Removing or restricting one account does not, by itself, establish what happened to the other sources.

For a business, the distinction matters when reports arrive from different people. A customer may describe a message from an apparent executive (PDF), while a supplier reports finding an unfamiliar site. Those observations may be connected, but they should not be treated as proof that every appearance has the same operator or can be addressed in the same way. The first useful question is what each person actually encountered: an account, a site, or material published within one of them.

Frankie Lee, founder of ContentRemoval.com, built the business after helping friends whose private images and videos had been shared without their consent. Their difficulty obtaining help prompted the former boxing trainer’s move into online content removal.

That experience shaped the company’s mission: protecting people and brands from harmful online content. Executive impersonation presents a different problem from the one that prompted his early work, but both call for attention to the material’s actual sources.

How cloned sites and copied identity material can mislead

A site made to resemble a company’s official presence can give a false profile somewhere to point. A copied executive photograph, biography or company logo may make the site appear familiar to a visitor who has seen the genuine business before.

The same material can also circulate on accounts that do not use the company’s exact name. The risk lies in the apparent relationship among these pieces: a visitor may see repeated identity details and assume the destinations are connected to the real executive.

Consider a hypothetical partner checking a message that appears to come from a founder. The profile names the founder, and its description points to a site displaying copied company material. The partner’s concern is not limited to whether the profile looks convincing.

They may need to decide whether a request, introduction or business proposal comes from someone authorized to speak for the company. Uncertainty at that point can interrupt a commercial conversation and require time from the people who manage security and external communications.

Copied material can also outlast the account that first drew attention. A photograph or biography might remain on a separate page after a profile has been removed. That does not mean every copy carries the same risk. Placement and context matter: material presented as an official point of contact has different implications from material that merely mentions an executive. A useful assessment looks at how each appearance could be understood by the people likely to encounter it.

Why resolving one source may leave exposure elsewhere

Account, site and content describe different parts of the problem. An account is a presence on a platform. A site is a web destination. Content is the photograph, text, logo or other material published through either one. One piece of content can appear in several places, while a single site can contain multiple misleading elements. This plain distinction helps a company describe what remains visible after any one item is addressed.

It also prevents confusion between removing material at its source and removing a search result. Source removal concerns the underlying post, account or page. Search delisting concerns whether a particular result appears through a search service; it does not necessarily remove the material from the website hosting it. Conversely, addressing a source does not automatically establish that every copy or reference elsewhere has been resolved. Neither action should be described as a universal fix for an impersonation case.

A business therefore needs a fuller picture than a count of search results or a screenshot of the first fake profile. A result may point to a source, a copied page, or a page discussing the issue. Each has a different role in the exposure. The relevant question is which sources could still cause someone to mistake an unauthorized presence for an official one. That keeps attention on the false identity rather than on visibility alone.

What a coordinated assessment should establish

When several sources are involved, a coordinated assessment brings the account, site and content findings together. It should establish which appearances claim to represent the executive or business, which identity details have been copied, and whether the same material appears across separate destinations. It should also distinguish content controlled by a platform from pages hosted elsewhere. These differences affect what can realistically be assessed for removal and which issues may need the company’s security or communications team to address.

That work is more useful when it is guided by the likely audience for each false presence. A fake profile contacting partners creates a different immediate concern from a copied biography sitting on a little-used page. A cloned site that appears to invite business inquiries raises questions about who may mistake it for an authorized channel. Assessing those concerns together can help a company decide where specialist attention is most relevant without assuming that every appearance will have the same outcome.

ContentRemoval.com provides online content removal services for people and businesses facing harmful material across web and social platforms. In an impersonation matter, a specialist assessment can examine the affected sources and the options available for each. It cannot make a blanket promise that every account, page, or copy will disappear. The value is in treating the exposure as a connected set of sources rather than closing the case when the first visible item is addressed.

Matching the response to the scope of the problem

For founders and executives, the commercial harm of impersonation can begin before anyone can measure its full reach. A customer who questions whether a message is genuine may delay a decision. A partner who finds competing versions of an executive’s identity may have to seek confirmation through another channel. Security and communications staff may then need to respond to concerns while establishing which online presences are actually involved. A clear account of the sources makes that conversation more precise.

The most useful description of a case separates the affected accounts, the sites they reference and the identity material appearing on each. It also notes which appearances seem to present themselves as official, rather than treating every mention of the executive as equivalent. That distinction helps a business explain its concern and understand what a professional assessment needs to cover.

When a false identity appears across several destinations, a coordinated assessment can establish which sources warrant attention and what removal work may be appropriate. The aim is a response matched to the actual exposure: one that recognizes the difference between addressing a profile, addressing a website and addressing copies that may remain elsewhere.

item.title: SplitSecure Launches New Access Control Architecture for Humans and AI Agents
item.description:
San Francisco, United States, November 23rd, 2026, CyberNewswire

SplitSecure, the cybersecurity technology provider, today unveiled a new access control platform based on secret splitting technology. The platform is intended to replace traditional access controls tools such as password managers, PAM, and vaults. On launch, it supports passwords, passkeys, one-time codes, SAML & OIDC federation, SSH, x.509 CA, OpenPGP, code signing (Nitro, Google Chrome Extensions), and general secrets vaulting.

The platform is intended for secure organizations of all sizes, including both large enterprise plans and a free plan for teams of up to six.

The access control space today contains a wide variety of tools. A secure organization would typically require a password manager, MFA app, vault, certificate manager, and PAM, among other tools. But despite their variety, all these tools use a common architecture where clients’ secrets are stored in a singular “vault”. It is this architecture SplitSecure seeks to disrupt, with a new way of storing and using secrets based on secret-splitting.

Secret splitting is the practice of breaking secrets across multiple devices rather than storing them in one location. This has been common practice in classified government environments for over thirty years but has historically been seen as high-effort and has had only limited adoption in industry. SplitSecure’s new platform is a significant advance of the state of the art, offering a ready-to-use implementation of techniques that were previously limited to advanced security teams in elite organizations.

Because of this general advancement, SplitSecure is able to replicate the functionality of many common tools. Its new platform provides password management, MFA, vaulting, certificate signing, and more PAM functionality such as shared accounts and resources. Supported resource types include passwords, passkeys, one-time codes, SAML 2.0 sign-ons, secrets, certificates, SSH certificates, signing keys, OpenPGP identities, and crypto wallets.

This new technology also offers the particular advantage that it cryptographically guarantees the service provider has no access to client’s secrets. This is in contrast to traditional PAM tools, in which the provider holds the “keys to the kingdom” at all times and a compromised vendor may be able to compromise client information.

Tristan Morris, CEO of SplitSecure, commented: “We were very ambitious we wanted a tool where people didn’t have to trust us as the provider, whereby design they’re the custodians of their own secrets. But we also wanted it to be so easy to use you could imagine a non-technical person using it instead of a password manager. We’ve done that, and it’s amazing to see it launch.”

He also noted that SplitSecure’s new platform integrates with common identity providers for an easier transition. “It should always be easy to set up,” he said. “Migration, first time setup, our goal was for that to take under half an hour.” Details on supported security and privacy frameworks are available in the SplitSecure Trust Center.

The free plan of SplitSecure’s new platform, which is available to all customers now, offers access control with the following key differentiators:

  1. Modern Privileged Access: Zero trust, just-in-time access, zero standing privilege, on-demand step-up authentication, multi-party approvals, and quantum resistance come as standard.
  2. Condenses Multiple Tools: SplitSecure can condense two to five tools in the security stack.
  3. No-Vendor-Threat Architecture: Root keys are held exclusively by the customer, so SplitSecure as the vendor has no access to customer secrets.
  4. Built-In Audit and Compliance: Every privileged action are logged automatically with full context on every plan. Paid plans can view the logs for security analysis and forensics.

About SplitSecure

SplitSecure is a cybersecurity technology provider, established to develop and modernize secret splitting technology. After being founded in 2025 by Tristan Morris and Marc Tremblay, it raised $4.7M from Cowboy, Twelve Below, and Cofound Ventures. Its access control platform combines PAM, password and passkey management, secrets vaulting, and auditing in one product, with root keys held exclusively by the customer. 

SplitSecure’s new access control platform is free for teams of up to six. Learn more at splitsecure.com or read the documentation.

item.title: Malicious Google Ads Target Mac Users with Fake Codex and Claude Code Downloads
item.description:
Cato Networks researchers investigating malicious Google ads found fake downloads for Codex, Claude Code and Homebrew in malicious sponsored search results appearing under the verified identities of legitimate businesses with no apparent connection to the software.

In research shared with Hackread.com, Cato researchers noted capturing a fake Codex ad under the profile of a health and nutrition business that also advertised the company’s own products. The Codex ad also contained wording from its health-related promotions. “A mismatch in the ads stood out,” Cato Networks noted in the blog post.

Cato believes the attackers either phished the advertisers’ Google Ads accounts or misused their identities for running this campaign, which means the firm “may also be a victim.”

Researchers followed a Google ad shown for the search “claude code mac download” and found that it eventually led to a ClickFix attack (in which a user is tricked into running a malicious command and gets the device infected).

In that case, the search generated ads that redirected visitors to parentpreneurxcom, where they were asked to copy a command into macOS Terminal to install the software.

Interestingly, this redirect didn’t show everyone the same page. item.title: How to Use Camera Tracking to Make Your Videos More Dynamic
item.description:
Most videos you film yourself have one problem: the camera never moves. Even with a tripod to stabilize the shot, after a few seconds, the clip can feel quite flat.

Videos with a professional touch are more appealing to watch. Because it involves following the subject, zooming on significant things, and shifting the scene. But what if everything is already shot?

That is where camera tracking comes into play. It allows you to introduce motion during editing, rather than having to reshoot. In this guide, we’ll tell you how it works, break down the steps, and give you 6 easy ways to enhance your videos.

What Camera Tracking Does to a Static Shot

Camera tracking converts a static shot taken with a camera into a moving camera shot. The editor ‘trails’ the shot to match the movement of a given target.

Say you are walking across the room; for instance, your frame can simply follow you rather than displaying the whole room to you. For you, it will seem to be more like a true-life video.

Camera tracking vs. motion tracking: Camera tracking moves the frame to track your subject. Motion tracking moves text, stickers, or other objects along with something in the video.

The Tool We’ll Use: Filmora Camera Tracking

Let’s get started with editing videos! This tutorial uses Wondershare Filmora, a desktop video editor that supports Mac and Windows.

Here’s the thing: Automatic camera tracking will follow moving subjects and ensure that they stay in-frame – all without manually keyframing.

Filmora offers three tracking modes:

  • Head Tracking: Locks onto a person’s head. Very useful in interviews, lessons, and talking-head footage.
  • Body Tracking: Tracks movement of the entire body. Good for walking videos, dances, sports, and workouts.
  • Custom Target: Choose what to track, from pets to products to a moving subject.

Additionally, Filmora allows you to easily perfect your output: You can see a preview of the tracking, reposition the framing, or clear the result and do the tracking again.

And the greatest part of all? You can split, trim, resize, and copy the supported tracked clips without removing the tracking results. So, there is no need to re-apply the tracking.

Other Tracking Features of Filmora

Auto Subject Tracking

It will track the movement of the subject, automatically keeping them in frame. If a person walks across the room or at a speaker’s pace while giving a presentation, the subject remains more in frame with automatic tracking.

Smooth Camera Movement

Make your “Follow the Camera” videos a cinematically lively experience. Filmora seamlessly pans on objects as they move, so walking vlogs, fitness tutorials, and product reviews will have a professional, attractive look.

Preview and Adjust Tracking

Once‍‍‍ the tracking is done, have a look at how your picture looks and, if necessary, adjust the framing. Some of the supported adjustment parameters give you a real-time preview so that you can make changes and see the result ‍‍‍instantly.

After tracking, you can also split, trim, resize, and copy clips while retaining tracking results for supported objects. Filmora provides several tracking features that are simple to use, including Motion Tracking, Planar Tracking, Auto Reframe, and more.

Step-by-Step: Add Camera Movement to a Tripod Shot

Would‍‍‍ you like your still footage to appear livelier? Here’s a three-step guide on how to utilize the Camera Tracking function in Filmora.

Launch Filmora on your computer, set up a New Project, then click Import and choose the file to upload your video.

Step 2. Camera Tracking Mode Selection

To run camera tracking from the selected clip, just click Video > Tracking > Camera Tracking.

Turn on the camera tracking feature and choose which one among Head, Body, or Custom you wish tracking to follow.

Modify the settings, then click Start. During the process, the software will be able to detect the motion and then move the frame to keep up with the action.

Step 3. Watch the Video, Adjust Camera Settings, and Export It

After completing the camera tracking function, you can play the video to see if the camera moves with the subject very smoothly from corner to corner.

6 Ways to Use Camera Tracking for More Dynamic Edits

Camera tracking isn’t only about tracking a moving subject. You can use it to switch between different camera angles, to focus on specific shots, and to liven up simple footage.

1. Make a Follow Shot

Utilize Body Tracking to track someone walking in the frame. Having the person always in the center of the shot provides the sensation of a moving camera in a still wide shot.

Try it on: Travel vlogs and store walkthroughs.

2. Switch Between Wide and Close-Up Shots

Duplicate your tracked clip but leave one version wide and zoom in on the other. Cut between the two to give an impression of two camera angles, even though it was shot in one.

Try it on: Tutorials and interviews.

3. Change Framing at Important Moments

Break it when your tracked clip hits a key moment, like a funny face or a product reveal. Zoom in for that moment to help keep viewers’ attention.

Try it on: Product reveals and storytelling videos.

4. Leave Space in Front of Moving Subjects

Move the framing so there’s some space in front of the moving subject rather than perfectly in the middle. Just that little bit of space is enough to make movement seem more natural and cinematic.

Try it on: Running, cycling, and dancing videos.

5. Keep Products in Focus

Use Custom Target tracking to follow the product when you grab it, rotate it, or move it across the table. The frame will follow the product so that the viewer can focus on the product.

Try it on: Unboxing videos and product demonstrations.

6. Combine Camera Tracking With B-Roll

Flip between your tracked main video and still B-Roll footage. For instance, I will video myself walking through a store, then cut away to close-up shots of products. This adds visual interest to the finished piece.

Try it on: Travel videos, product reviews, and lifestyle content.

Common Mistakes That Make Camera Tracking Look Fake

Camera tracking can be very effective, but a few errors can ruin the shot.

Using low-resolution footage: When you zoom in too much, low-resolution video will look blurry. If possible, use high-resolution footage.

Losing the subject: If a subject moves off entirely, then the tracking may fail. Crop that area out of the shot or track again.

Tracking in busy scenes: Filmora may follow the wrong person or object. Choose what you wish to track with Custom Target.

Cropping‍‍‍ too tight: A very close crop makes everything small look like a shake or a tremor. It’s a good idea to leave a little space around your subject that allows the tracking to look smooth.

You don’t necessarily have to shoot only on track. You should mix moving shots and fixed shots to emphasize the highlights of your ‍‍‍video.

Filming Tips That Make Tracking Easier

Good camera tracking starts with good footage. Here are a few simple tips to get better results:

  • Shoot with more space: Give extra space to your subject so you can crop and adjust the frame. Record in 4K if possible.
  • Even lighting: Illuminate your subject well so the tracking feature can pick up movements faster.
  • Subject in view: Ensure that the person or item stays within the original frame until the end of the clip.
  • No strong backlight: Capturing your subject against the light might make the person too dark and less trackable.
  • Choose a simple background: Avoid crowded backgrounds that might confuse the tracker or cause it to follow the wrong object.

Closing

There’s no need for costly camera equipment to get more variety in your videos. Simply add one tripod shot and add camera tracking to bring you forward, backwards and side to side in one take. Want to try it out? Use your most static video from last week and switch between wide shots and close-ups. Practice using this easy tool to grab your viewer’s attention.

item.title: UK Retailer Next Discloses Cyber Incident at Online Supplier
item.description:
British fashion and retail companies are facing a difficult year on the cybersecurity front, with incidents involving major brands like ASOS, Phase Eight, Hobbs and Whistles being reported lately. The latest retailer to report a cyber incident is clothing and homeware company Next, which has disclosed unauthorised access to company information through one of its online suppliers.

The Enderby, Leicestershire-based Next published an official breach notification on November 23, explaining that attackers had gained access to some information held by one of its online suppliers, but it did not name the supplier or disclose what information was accessed. The company also clarified that its own systems had not been breached.

What Happened at Next

According to the official notice, Next learned about the incident from its supplier and immediately initiated an investigation in collaboration with the impacted supplier, law enforcement and other relevant agencies. The company hasn’t revealed the date of the attack or when the supplier first discovered it. More details may emerge as the investigation progresses.

The retailer did confirm that there was no evidence that customer personal information had been affected, explaining that the information accessed was limited and cannot be used to commit fraud against the company or its customers.

“Our investigations are ongoing; however, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised,” Next stated in the notice. “Despite the limited and benign nature of the affected data, we are treating the matter with the utmost seriousness and are working closely with the supplier, law enforcement, and relevant regulatory authorities.”

Next did not ask customers to take any action in its announcement.

Why Retailers Should Pay Attention

Cybercriminals appear to be finding ways to affect fashion and retail businesses through different types of attacks. Hackread.com recently reported the ASOS incident, in which attackers hijacked the retailer’s mobile app notifications to send threatening messages to customers, and the company warned about attackers accessing customer names and contact details through third-party platforms.

In October, an attack disrupted IT systems at TFG London, the owner of Phase Eight, Hobbs and Whistles. The company was also investigating whether customer and employee information had been accessed.

These recent incidents make it all the more important for retailers to protect information held by third parties. As we’ve been observing, a breach doesn’t necessarily have to start inside a retailer’s own network anymore. Suppliers usually have access to company information, customer records, or systems used to run everyday services, so it becomes crucial to safeguard this data properly.

Next has reported a limited incident, with no current evidence of customer data being affected. That is different from the problems reported by ASOS and TFG. But the incident itself shows that retailers cannot rely only on the security of their own systems- they need to know how well the companies handling their information protect it.

Experts Warn of Further Risks to Retailers and Customers

Sharing their views with Hackread.com, cybersecurity experts warned that the incident should not be dismissed simply because Next has found no evidence of customer data being compromised.

Donnan Mallon, threat intelligence analyst at Talion Cyber Security, said:

“Following the recent spate of attacks on UK retailers, this regulatory notice highlights that a partner of Next is the latest victim. We don’t know who the third party is, or whether the data of other organisations has been impacted, but Next does say it feels confident no customer data has been compromised. This is reassuring but it doesn’t mean customers of Next should throw caution to the wind. Breach forensics can quickly change situations, often unearthing that attacks are far more severe than initial assumptions.”

“This means customers of Next must be wary of correspondence just now regardless of how it reaches them. Threat actors will typically hijack on publicity surrounding attacks to target victims, so customers of Next should treat any updates on the attack with caution. It’s much safer to visit Next’s own website for notices on the breach.”

William Wright, CEO at Closed Door Security, also pointed to the wider supply-chain risk, saying:

“This marks another in a spate of cyberattacks targeting UK retailers and their supply chains; extensive details have not been released about Next’s investigation, but the company’s internal systems have allegedly not been affected. Even if this attack does ultimately turn out to be minor, it represents another point in a continuing escalation of cyberattacks on the UK and global retail sector, a trend which has worried lawmakers and dented consumer confidence.”

“The security of third parties and of supply chains has come into focus as a major weakness in many organizations’ resilience and security planning, but tackling this is difficult because it’s systemic. There’s no way for organizations to ensure all their partners are secure, and breaches of single firms can cascade across sectors depending on their market share and exposure.”

“Next has cautioned that no personal data relating to customers has been leaked, but customers should remain wary and on guard about potential phishing related to the attack: announcements like this come with the risk that attackers might attempt to impersonate affected companies, and worry around attacks can lead people to lower their guard and follow fraudulent links more readily.”

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: When Threat Intelligence Works Against Your SOC: 3 Patterns to Watch For
item.description:
Disclosure: This article was provided by ANY.RUN. The information and analysis presented are based on their research and findings

It wouldn’t be much of an exaggeration to say that threat intelligence, which is supposed to help security teams detect threats earlier, can sometimes have the opposite effect on SOC efficiency.

Poorly selected or implemented threat intelligence sources can introduce new operational challenges and add friction to daily workflows.

Here are three reasons why your threat intelligence might be working against your SOC, and what you can do about it.

Pattern #1. Relying on Threat Data with Limited Coverage and Quality

With SIEM, EDR, and other security systems collecting telemetry, identifying suspicious activity, and helping analysts investigate potential threats, it’s important to remember that these tools primarily provide visibility into your own environment.

External visibility starts with intelligence about malicious infrastructure observed elsewhere. Without it, your SOC risks acting with limited visibility: a threat targets companies in another industry, but you only become aware of it when it reaches your organization.

To break this cycle, you can use external threat intelligence sources. But there’s another problem: their data may be outdated, low-quality, or overlap significantly with what you already have.

How Do You Break This Pattern?

Incorporate threat intelligence derived from real-world malware and phishing investigations across different industries. This helps expand visibility beyond your own environment and provides early warnings about malicious infrastructure observed elsewhere.

For example, ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox can serve as a source of threat data, collecting malicious indicators from real-world malware and phishing analyses across a community of more than 16,000 organizations worldwide.

These indicators are delivered to your SIEM/SOAR/XDR and other systems through Threat Intelligence Feeds (TI Feeds), giving SOC teams access to malicious IP addresses, domains, and URLs observed across different industries.

With approximately 99% unique IOCs compared with other threat intelligence sources and a near-zero false positive rate, ANY.RUN TI Feeds help expand coverage without overwhelming analysts with duplicate or irrelevant data.

Expand your SOC’s threat intelligence coverage

Support detection in your existing stack with threat data from 16,000+ SOCs worldwide.

Explore TI Feeds

Pattern #2. Getting Threat Intelligence Too Late

Threat intelligence has a limited window of opportunity. The speed at which intelligence reaches security systems is an important factor in detection effectiveness.

An organization that receives information about malicious infrastructure earlier has a better opportunity to identify matching activity before an incident develops further. It’s all about how quickly new intelligence becomes available to your security stack.

How Do You Break This Pattern?

Continuously updated intelligence that can be delivered into detection systems with minimal delay is the only way to keep up with an ever-changing threat landscape.

ANY.RUN’s research illustrates why this matters. In a study of malicious indicators identified during Interactive Sandbox investigations, approximately 30% of unique malicious IOCs were already present in ANY.RUN TI Feeds before the corresponding investigations began.

item.title: Researchers Disrupt Massive BADBOX 3.0 Ad Fraud and Proxy Botnet
item.description:
A years-long ad fraud operation targeting cheap, uncertified Android TV boxes, streaming devices and other consumer devices has suffered another major disruption. Digital fraud and bot-defense firm HUMAN reports that its Satori Threat Intelligence team has disrupted BADBOX 3.0, in which the peak volume reached was around 40 billion ad bid requests a day.

This represents over 4% of connected TV (CTV) traffic observed by researchers. Also, it is three times higher than the volume of the previous record-holder, VASTFLUX.

How BADABOX 3.0 Scheme Works

The BADBOX 3.0 campaign started with malware hidden inside cheap Android streaming boxes and tablets, which then connected those infected devices into a large botnet controlled by criminals. This was a coordinated effort involving spreading BADBOX 3.0 malware, playing fake ads, and selling victims’ home internet connections for profit.

The malware ran video ads in a hidden window, which means the device was playing ads even though nothing appeared on the screen, whereas the ad requests seemed to be coming from legitimate streaming apps. This misled advertisers into paying for traffic that was never genuine.

Researchers linked its malware module catalog to Chinese electronics manufacturer TXCZ through device software, domains, server infrastructure and code repositories. They also noted that the malware turned infected devices into residential proxy nodes across 11 networks. This allowed outsiders to use a victim’s home internet connection to route their own traffic while creating an illusion that it was coming from an ordinary household and conceal their actual location.

BADBOX keeps coming back

Hackread.com first reported on BADBOX in October 2023 when researchers at HUMAN found backdoors on cheap Android TV boxes and tablets. The malware was already installed before the devices reached buyers, leaving them compromised from the moment they were switched on. HUMAN found more than 74,000 infected devices while the PEACHPIT component was being used to commit ad fraud.

By July 2025, BADBOX had returned on a much larger scale with BADBOX 2.0 infecting more than 10 million devices across 222 countries and territories. It came with a new backdoor, BB2DOOR, which gave operators ways to commit click fraud, manipulate ads and sell access to victims’ internet connections. The campaign led to a disruption effort involving Google and other partners.

BADBOX 3.0 is different from the previous versions as instead of keeping all its malware in one place, it fetches new modules from public code repositories via a C2 server. It also hosts backup copies on other platforms and content delivery networks (CDNs) in case files get removed. That allows operators to replace malware and keep devices working for them. Some of the fake ad traffic was also created without an infected device, using bogus server-side ad insertion (SSAI) requests (called SSAI spoofing).

Researchers also believe IpMoYu, a residential proxy network exposed during the BADBOX 2.0 investigation, has returned as PXYEDGE. The new service advertised around 200,000 nodes, while monitoring recorded as many as 340,000 unique connections across its services.

The latest disruption is a huge blow, but BADBOX’s history offers little reason to assume its operators will stop here. We’ve seen the operation getting disrupted, then returning, the infrastructure moving, and the fraud evolving. Cheap devices with questionable software and little security oversight remain an easy way back in.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Free vs. Paid Security Tools: Where Free Options Fall Short
item.description:
Many free security tools offer solid protection, helping companies detect and block threats and keep daily operations secure. For small businesses, startups, and independent companies with limited IT budgets, these tools are a practical way to keep cybersecurity costs under control without leaving gaps in protection.

Identifying the differences between free cybersecurity tools and paid software may prove to be very useful for business people to make informed decisions about securing their systems, employees, and data.

Free Tools Cover Prevention Better Than Most Owners Think 

This is an era of advanced free cybersecurity tools. New firms no longer need to pay for sophisticated software to protect themselves from potential threats. However, many free applications can offer multiple security tools such as:

  • Antivirus Software: This software helps identify and detect known viruses and isolate and remove malware.
  • Password Managers: For storing employee/user login information and ensuring passwords are not reused.
  • Firewalls: These can be used for monitoring traffic to the network and controlling access to it.
  • Browser security extension: Helps users avoid accessing harmful websites and informs the user regarding any suspicious links on the site.
  • The other kinds of security methods utilized by companies are multi-factor authentication.

Using free software for small business cybersecurity can lead to increased security. There are various free software options for account protection and secure communications.

The Gaps Show Up After the Alert, Not Before It 

Prevention is merely a tactic within cybersecurity. If it circumvents any of these defenses, businesses must grasp what is going on, the seriousness of the incident, and what steps will be taken to minimize the effects. Common limitations include:

  • One-way investigation: Limited investigations that do not attempt to detail how an attacker got in or which systems have been impacted can be performed with free software.
  • No fixed response (business) team: The business team may find themselves in a situation where they are tasked with taking action without technical expertise.
  • No continuous monitoring: There are free solutions that do not provide continuous monitoring, so you have to check alerts yourself.
  • Not enough reporting: The detailed history of incidents and security analytics/compliance reports are only available through paid subscriptions.

The FBI 2025 Internet Crime Report stated that the Internet Crime Complaint Center received over one million complaints, with losses on the verge of $21 billion. That’s up from a year ago when that figure was $16.6 billion.

What You’re Paying For Is Response Time 

In addition, paid cybersecurity services may offer further security measures such as:

  • Continuous security monitoring.
  • Vulnerability assessments.
  • Professional incident response.
  • Detailed security reporting.
  • Technical and recovery assistance.
  • Special training in advanced threat detection and investigation.

Think about the impact of an employee opening an email attachment with a link that leads to malicious content. Suspicious activity may be caught by a simple free program, and an alert may be sent. But a more full-blown commercial offering may make a difference:

  • Determine the source of the threat.
  • Segment the device that is affected.
  • Look into possible compromise of other systems.
  • Identify if information is sensitive and if it has been released.
  • Help with recovery and help ensure that similar incidents never happen again.

Rapid response is critical because of the rapid growth that cyber incidents can experience. Cyber providers such as Cyber Husky can help by offering expertise without the burden of an in-house security team. 

Decide Control by Control, Not Tool by Tool 

It is wrong to assume that all free tools must go to make way for one paid tool, but it is right to ascertain your personal security requirements and know where additional protection will cost the company more. The following comparison may be helpful to begin:

A small business that manages relatively limited amounts of sensitive data might be OK accepting free software for some of its functions. For smaller businesses that hold customer records, financial data, or business-sensitive information, though, more extensive small business cybersecurity measures might be required. 

Conclusion 

Free cybersecurity products play a key part in business security nowadays. They provide inexpensive protection, which may assist you in creating a certain level of protection without having to create an expensive subscription. However, prevention is not the only solution. 

Organizations need to be capable of investigating any suspicious activities, responding to them, and recovering from them without causing too much disruption. If you do not know how vulnerable your current security protection system is, you can use that information to get a professional security evaluation.

item.title: Researchers Take Over Five US Treasury Subdomains for About $3 Each
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers at Intruder took control of five US Treasury subdomains for about $3 each by claiming Amazon Web Services (AWS) IP addresses that the subdomains still pointed to.

The researchers demonstrated that they could publish their own content on the affected addresses. Intruder did not report access to Treasury’s internal systems or theft of government data.

How old DNS records left the subdomains exposed

When an organisation retires a cloud server, its DNS records can still direct visitors to the server’s old IP address. If the cloud provider assigns that address to another customer, the new holder can serve content under the original subdomain. That leftover entry is known as a dangling DNS record.

In its research report, shared with Hackread.com, Intruder said it tested whether AWS Elastic IP addresses matched live DNS records. Over 48 hours, the researchers checked about 450,000 unique IP addresses and found 28 matches. Nearly half belonged to government organisations.

Five US Treasury subdomains pointed to addresses Intruder controlled:

  1. ftp.treasury.gov
  2. pcp.treasury.gov
  3. ww5.treasury.gov
  4. rdgw.treasury.gov
  5. irssearch.treasury.gov

Someone who gains control of a government subdomain could host a phishing page on a genuine .gov address and obtain a valid HTTPS certificate. Intruder also warned that older automated systems could still send credentials to a retired address, and that cookies configured to be shared with subdomains could be exposed. The report described these as risks and did not document credential or cookie theft.

AWS says customers are responsible for removing old DNS records

AWS blocked Intruder’s account from claiming or using Elastic IP addresses after 48 hours of testing. The researchers said they were still able to transfer addresses they had already claimed to another account within the same AWS organisation.

Intruder asked AWS to limit monthly IP allocations and apply restrictions to entire organisations. According to Intruder, AWS said on November 17 that it had no plans to make those changes and maintained that customers were responsible for removing obsolete DNS records.

Intruder said it notified the organisations affected by all 28 findings and that the DNS records were fixed. Its test covered 0.56% of AWS’s published EC2 IPv4 address space. For organisations retiring cloud services, the practical step is to remove or update the DNS records before releasing the addresses they point to.
